newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU makes timid moves in fight against child sex.
newsitem.headline: EU makes timid moves in fight against child sex.

text.p: The European Union, responding to a Belgian child-sex murder scandal that has made headlines round the world, agreed timid steps on Friday to discourage the sexual exploitation of children.

Justice ministers meeting in Brussels agreed a definition of sexual exploitation of children, pledged "dissuasive criminal penalties" for convicted paedophiles and said they would make pornographic material involving minors a crime.

It was "an important date and a victory for the protection of children", French Justice Minister Jacques Toubon said but European Commission and diplomats stressed the text agreed had been considerably watered down.
The ministers confirmed an earlier agreement bringing the EU's police agency Europol into the fight against the trade in children and women.

They said the EU would also set up, through the Hague-based agency, a system allowing EU countries to pool experts in fighting the trade and agreed police officers should take part in exchange training courses.
But faced with opposition from the Netherlands, the ministers failed in particular to agree to punish the "personal use" of pornographic material featuring children.

Both Belgium and Germany had fought to keep the clause making "possession for personal use" of, for example, paedophile videos a crime but the final text effectively leaves EU states free to decide for themselves how far to go in prohibiting such material.
The ministers also shied away from aligning their laws to make "sex tourism" a criminal offence, which would have allowed the prosecution of EU nationals who go overseas for child sex.
A significant number of EU countries currently only agree to this if the country where the offence was committed has similar legislation -- the so-called double criminality requirement.
In practice, the action agreed on Friday leaves EU states to continue with their own policies and legislation, although some countries like Belgium France and Luxembourg pledged to go further.
"France will abolish double criminality provisions...this will allow for the arrest of a person for a crime committed in another country," a French diplomat said.
